opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The reading from the Book of Daniel presents a powerful moment of humility. The people acknowledge that they have nothing left to offer God—no prince, no prophet, no temple sacrifices, no incense, no place to present first fruits. All the outward signs of worship are gone. Yet in that emptiness they recognize something deeper: what God truly desires is not ritual alone, but a contrite heart and a humble spirit. Even when everything else has been stripped away, the human heart can still turn back to God in honesty and repentance.

Immediately after this comes the Gospel from Gospel of Matthew 18:21–35, where Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive. Jesus answers with the parable of the unforgiving servant. In the story, a servant is forgiven an enormous and impossible debt by his master. Yet the very same servant refuses to forgive a fellow servant who owes him only a small amount. Instead of showing the mercy he received, he demands payment and has the man thrown into prison. The master, hearing of this, is outraged and reminds him that mercy should have produced mercy.

Taken together, the readings reveal something important about the human heart. In Daniel, we see what it means to approach God with humility, recognizing our need for mercy. In the Gospel, we see how easily we can forget that mercy once it has been given to us. We can become like the wicked servant—grateful when forgiveness is extended to us, yet reluctant to extend that same forgiveness to others.

The message is clear and challenging. When we remember how much we have been forgiven, gratitude naturally leads to mercy. But when we forget, our hearts can quickly harden. These readings remind us to remain humble, selfless, and grateful in every circumstance, always ready to forgive as we ourselves have been forgiven.
